rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the risk of non-elution. The retention window will guide subsequent slope and temperature experiments.
Injection 1 already achieves the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient one step to seek a faster fully resolved method and measure the critical pair's sensitivity to slope.
The shorter gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves the critical pair close to the resolution threshold. Raise temperature at the same slope to test whether selectivity permits further acceleration.

At 50 C all pairs retain a useful resolution margin and the last peak elutes earlier. Shorten the gradient another step to test the speed limit while retaining injection 3 as a maximum-score fallback.

Narrow the solvent window to restore a shallower slope and improve the critical pair while retaining the six-minute programmed gradient. Starting at 0.15 should remove some low-organic waiting time without making the earliest peaks unretained.

Shift the window upward while preserving the successful gradient slope to shorten retention further. This tests whether the early pair can tolerate stronger starting solvent without losing full resolution.

Reduce the endpoint one grid step to make the gradient slightly shallower and recover the critical pair's small resolution deficit. This should retain much of injection 6's speed advantage over the fastest fully resolved method.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention while narrowing the window enough to protect the slope-sensitive critical pair. Monitor the earliest pair closely because stronger starting solvent may compress it.

Injection 8's last peak eluted near 0.49 organic, so a 0.60 endpoint should still cover the elution window. This four-minute gradient is only slightly steeper and may shorten the run while preserving full resolution.

Test the upper temperature limit at the fastest fully resolved solvent program to assess further time savings and temperature-driven selectivity changes. Maximum CRF is already secured, so this run can probe whether reordered pairs offer a faster operating window.

Test a much steeper gradient to see whether the slope-sensitive middle pair separates again after an elution-order reversal, enabling a substantially faster method. Returning to 40 C should provide more selectivity for the early pair than the higher temperatures.

Probe the steep-gradient regime at low temperature, which may separate the middle pair on the opposite side of its apparent order reversal. Lowering the starting organic fraction also protects early retention while allowing the steepest available gradient.

Test an intermediate temperature with a slope between injections 6 and 7 to seek full resolution at a shorter retention time. The lower starting organic fraction should protect the early pair better than the 0.25 start used at 60 C.

Test a stronger starting solvent with a shallower gradient to balance shorter retention against middle-pair resolution. Lowering temperature to 45 C should help protect the early pair, which became limiting at higher temperatures.

Lower the starting organic fraction from injection 13 to recover early-pair resolution at 55 C. The slightly steeper gradient should offset some added retention time, testing a nearby route to a fast, maximum-CRF method.

Return to 50 C, where the early pair remains resolved, and test a slope just steeper than injection 9. This probes whether its small middle-pair resolution margin can yield a further reduction in last-peak time.

Back off the slope after injection 16's small resolution failure and lower the starting organic fraction to strengthen early-pair separation. This targets a four-minute program with more resolution margin than the fastest maximum-CRF method.

Test one temperature step below injection 17 while keeping its solvent program fixed. The middle pair has some resolution margin, and lower temperature may improve early-pair separation enough to provide a more robust maximum-score method.

Test a two-minute gradient with a shallower slope to preserve middle-pair resolution, followed by the endpoint hold. The final peaks will likely elute during the hold; this checks whether the shortest programmed gradient can still achieve maximum CRF without pushing the last peak beyond ten minutes.

Test one temperature step below the fastest fully resolved method, injection 9, to quantify its temperature sensitivity. Cooling should improve early-pair separation, while this run will establish whether the middle pair retains full resolution.

Preserve injection 19's successful gradient slope but extend it to a higher endpoint so the last peak avoids the slow hold at 0.40 organic. This targets maximum CRF with more resolution margin than injection 9 and a shorter elution time than injection 19.

Lower temperature one step from injection 21 to improve the limiting early pair while retaining its shallower gradient. The middle pair's resolution margin should accommodate modest cooling, potentially yielding a more robust maximum-CRF method.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 22 to shorten elution while using its middle-pair resolution margin. This should offer a faster maximum-CRF method at 45 C, with better early-pair separation than at 50 C.

Test a slope between injections 6 and 7, near the estimated middle-pair resolution threshold. This may slightly improve on the fastest fully resolved method while preserving the stronger early-pair separation of a 0.20 start.

Trim injection 21's endpoint and duration while preserving its successful slope and temperature. All peaks should remain inside the gradient, retaining maximum CRF and its resolution margin with a shorter programmed gradient.
